themes.theme: Codes of practice and codes of conduct as shared instruments
themes.definition: Voluntary codes drawn up under EU facilitation, and the taskforces they create, that put providers, deployers and authorities on a common set of measures.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires the AI Office to 'encourage and facilitate' codes of practice at Union level, 'taking into account international approaches' (#089; recital #046), and per the coder note such codes are a way for general-purpose model providers to show compliance. The AI Office may invite all general-purpose model providers and national competent authorities to take part, with civil society, industry, academia, downstream providers and independent experts able to support (#090). The Commission may also encourage codes on detecting and labelling AI-generated content (#050), and the Commission and Member States should facilitate voluntary codes of conduct on AI literacy with stakeholders (#068). The transparency Code of Practice (EU121) is one such instrument and creates its own coordination: signatories are encouraged to join a taskforce for sharing good practice (#242) and a task force on the EU icon open to researchers, civil society and national competent authorities (#246), and sectoral good practices drawn up by deployers and their associations 'will be made publicly available online' to enable monitoring by market surveillance authorities (#245). Who sets up, convenes or funds the taskforces is not stated (coder note on #242).
themes.holders: The AI Office; the Commission and Member States; general-purpose AI model providers; signatories of the transparency Code (providers and deployers) and their associations; national competent authorities and other stakeholders as participants.
themes.binding: Statutory duty on the AI Office to facilitate; the codes themselves are voluntary. Within EU121, 'will' binds signatories once they adhere, but adherence is voluntary, and taskforce participation is only encouraged. No consequence stated.

quotes.quote: The AI Office shall encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of practice at Union level in order to contribute to the proper application of this Regulation, taking into account international approaches.
The AI Office may invite all providers of general-purpose AI models, as well as relevant national competent authorities, to participate in the drawing-up of codes of practice.
Signatories are encouraged to actively participate in the taskforce that will be set up under the Code to facilitate the activities mentioned abo ve, the sharing of good practices

To ensure transparency, accountability and to enable monitoring by competent market surveillance authorities, sectoral good practices established in accordance with this paragraph will be made publicly available online.

themes.definition: Named persons or offices that other actors must or may address: authorised representatives of providers outside the EU, provider contact details for deployers, single points of contact in Member States, and contact roles inside EU institutions.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers of high-risk AI systems and of general-purpose AI models established outside the EU must, by written mandate and before placing their product on the EU market, appoint an authorised representative established in the Union (#071, #088; restated in the GPAI guidelines, #268), whom competent authorities can address 'in addition to or instead of the provider' on compliance (#072; recitals #035 and #036, which are two extracts of the same recital); per the coder note qualifying open-source models are exempt unless they present systemic risk (#088). The instructions for use must give the identity and contact details of the provider and any authorised representative (#067), which is the deployer's contact point. On the authority side, each Member State must designate a market surveillance authority as single point of contact (#121), 'vis-à-vis the public and other counterparts' per the recital (#060), and must make its Board representative a single contact point towards the Board and, where appropriate, stakeholders (#110); the GPAI guidelines invite providers to contact the AI Office 'immediately and proactively' (#262). Inside EU institutions, the European Court of Auditors has appointed an 'AI Act correspondent' as its primary contact with the EDPS, which the passage describes as the market surveillance authority for AI systems (#271), and Commission staff 'may always contact' the Central Intellectual Property Service for advice on intellectual property in outputs (#289).
themes.holders: Providers established in third countries and their authorised representatives; providers of high-risk systems (contact details); Member States and their designated market surveillance authorities and Board representatives; the AI Office; the ECA's AI Act correspondent; Commission staff and the Central Intellectual Property Service.
themes.binding: Statutory duties for authorised representatives and single points of contact (the coder notes point to fines under Art. 99(4)(b) and Art. 101, outside the passages); recitals 'should'; an internal appointment at the ECA; a permission ('may always') for Commission staff; an invitation in the GPAI guidelines.

quotes.quote: providers established in third countries shall, by written mandate, appoint an authorised representative which is established in the Union
Member States shall designate a market surveillance authority to act as the single point of contact for this Regulation

quotes.location: AI governance at the ECA, para 17 (p. 7)
quotes.quote: the ECA has appointed an “AI Act correspondent”, whose role is to act as the primary point of contact with the European Data Protection Supervisor (the market surveillance authority for AI systems).
For legal advice on intellectual property, Commission staff may always contact the Commission’s Central Intellectual Property Service – EC-IPR@ec.europa.eu

themes.theme: Dialogue between the AI Office and providers of general-purpose AI models
themes.definition: Formal and informal exchanges between the AI Office (or Commission) and providers of general-purpose AI models, alongside the formal enforcement procedures.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act lets the AI Office open a 'structured dialogue' with a model provider to gather information on internal testing and safeguards against systemic risk, and per the coder note similar dialogues precede information requests and measures (#025). The GPAI guidelines add a softer layer: the AI Office invites providers to contact it 'immediately and proactively' (#262), expects providers training models around 2 August 2025 to tell it 'how and when they will take the necessary steps to comply' (#263), and encourages 'close informal cooperation' during training, especially for models with systemic risk, 'to facilitate compliance and ensure timely market placement' (#270). The one hard duty is notification: a provider whose model meets or will meet the systemic-risk threshold must notify the Commission, per the note 'without delay and in any event within two weeks' (#269). The AI Office also says it will monitor and, 'if necessary', set out a common approach for external model evaluators, involving a network of evaluators (#264). [inference] The same office both encourages informal pre-market cooperation and supervises compliance; the passages do not say how these roles are kept apart.
themes.holders: The AI Office and the Commission; providers of general-purpose AI models, including those who modify models; a network of external evaluators and subject-matter experts.
themes.binding: Statutory power (#025) and statutory duty (#269; per the note, designation and possible fines under Art. 101); otherwise invitations, expectations ('should') and a conditional commitment ('if necessary').
themes.checks: Structured dialogue (#025): trigger, not stated in the passage; compared against, not stated; metric, not stated; who, the AI Office with the provider; result, information that may precede a request for access. Notification (#269): trigger, meeting the systemic-risk presumption threshold (the threshold value is not in these passages); who, the provider; result, not stated in the passage. External evaluation (#264): trigger, 'if necessary' after monitoring; comparator, metric and use of results not stated.

quotes.quote: the AI Office may initiate a structured dialogue with the provider of the general-purpose AI model to gather more information on the internal testing of the model, internal safeguards for preventing systemic risks
the provider must notify the Commission in line with Article 52(1) AI Act

The AI Office encourages close informal cooperation with providers during the training of their general-purpose AI models to facilitate compliance and ensure timely market placement, in particular for providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk.

The AI Office will monitor the situation and , if necessary, work to set out a common approach for external model evaluators, for instance, by involving the network of evaluators and other subject-matter experts.

themes.theme: Information duties along the AI value chain
themes.definition: Duties on providers and model developers to pass documentation, instructions and notices down the supply chain to deployers and downstream providers.
themes.what_is_set_out: High-risk AI systems must come with instructions for use giving 'the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance' (#032), known or foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks, so that 'the deployer is aware and takes them into account' (#031), the declared 'expected level of performance metrics', communicated 'in a clear and easily understandable way' (#033), and the provider's contact details (#067). Providers must tell distributors and, where applicable, deployers about corrective action (#070), and their quality management system must cover communication with authorities, notified bodies, operators and customers (#069). Providers of general-purpose models must draw up and keep up to date documentation for downstream providers that integrate the model, and for the AI Office and national authorities on request (#029, #043; restated in the GPAI guidelines, #266); open-source models keep their exemption only if they give at least their 'input and output modalities, capabilities, and limitations' (#261), and developers of open-source tools are encouraged to use model cards and data sheets (#040). The training-data Summary template asks modified or fine-tuned models to 'specify the model (version) name(s)' they build on and link to those models' Summaries (#211, #212), the only place in this cell where model versions are tracked. The EDPB opinion adds data-protection flows from developer to deployer: documentation on measures to reduce identification and on residual risks (#234), and notification of rectification or erasure (#235).
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk AI systems; providers of general-purpose AI models (including open-source and fine-tuning providers); developers of open-source tools; controllers developing models (EU074). Recipients are deployers, downstream providers, distributors and authorities.
themes.binding: Statutory where AI Act articles or Annex XII apply (the coder notes point to fines under Art. 99(4)(a) for #067 and #069); many passages on instructions for use are recitals ('should', 'urged'); the GPAI guidelines and EDPB opinion are interpretation; the Summary template field is mandatory 'where available'.
themes.checks: Declared performance (#033): trigger, placing the system on the market (the metrics go in the instructions for use); compared against, the provider's own declared 'expected level of performance'; metric, not specified in the passage; who, the provider declares and the deployer is to take it into account (#031); what happens if real performance falls short, not stated. No passage here requires a deployer to compare outputs with the declared metrics or to report back up the chain.

quotes.quote: The expected level of performance metrics should be declared in the accompanying instructions of use. Providers are urged to communicate that information to deployers in a clear and easily understandable way
an obligation to draw up and keep up to date documentation to be made available to downstream providers and , upon request, to the AI Office and the national competent authorities
specify the model (version) name(s) of that/those models and provide a link to their Summary(ies) where available.

the documentation provided to the controller(s) deploying the model and/or to data subjects, in particular the documentation related to the measures taken to reduce the likelihood of identification and regarding the possible residual risks.

themes.theme: Written agreements and cooperation duties between providers and their suppliers
themes.definition: Duties on suppliers of components and on earlier providers to give the provider of a high-risk system the information, access and help it needs, set down in written agreements.
themes.what_is_set_out: The provider of a high-risk AI system and any third party supplying 'an AI system, tools, services, components, or processes' used in it must, by written agreement, specify 'the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance based on the generally acknowledged state of the art' (#074; recitals #038, #039), and the Omnibus restates this with fines attached (#187). Per the coder notes, suppliers of free and open-source components other than general-purpose models are exempt, and the information covers training, retraining, testing, evaluation and integration. Where a system becomes high-risk through another party's change and that party becomes the new provider, the initial provider 'shall closely cooperate' and provide information and technical access (#073; recital #041), unless it clearly excluded that change; the Omnibus again restates with fines (#186). A recital asks providers of general-purpose AI systems to cooperate with high-risk providers and with the competent authorities (#037), and all of this is without prejudice to intellectual property and trade secrets (coder note on #073). [inference] A public body that substantially modifies or rebrands a system would become its provider and depend on these duties towards its supplier, but no passage here says so.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk AI systems; third-party suppliers of systems, tools, services, components or processes; initial providers; providers of general-purpose AI systems.
themes.binding: Statutory (Art. 25); the Omnibus adds administrative fines under a new Art. 99(4)(da) (#186, #187); recitals 'should'.
themes.checks: Not a check in itself. Per the note on #038 the information and access cover testing and evaluation, so these agreements supply what a provider needs in order to test, but no trigger, comparator, metric or use of results is stated.

quotes.quote: The provider of a high-risk AI system and the third party that supplies an AI system, tools, services, components, or processes that are used or integrated in a high-risk AI system shall, by written agreement, specify the necessary information
That initial provider shall closely cooperate with new providers and shall make available the necessary information and provide the reasonably expected technical access and other assistance

quotes.location: Art. 1(12)(b), replacing AI Act Art. 25(4) first…
quotes.quote: shall, by written agreement, specify the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance based on the generally acknowledged state of the art, in order to enable the provider of the high-risk AI system to fully comply

closely cooperate with the providers of the relevant high-risk AI systems to enable their compliance with the relevant obligations under this Regulation and with the competent authorities established under this Regulation.

themes.theme: Public bodies' procurement and contract terms with AI suppliers
themes.definition: What public bodies are told to require of AI suppliers through tenders, contracts, data agreements and requests for documentation, and the supplier terms that bind public deployers.
themes.what_is_set_out: The most specific passages come from the EDPS, addressing EU institutions. Its risk guidance asks procurement staff to coordinate with deployment staff (#216), tender specifications to require the tenderer's capability and, per the note, 'technical and procedural quality guarantees' (#217), and the organisation to invite the provider to produce documentation on the system, its explainability and its security (#219) and to 'request from the provider a set of metrics that will allow for the evaluation of the AI system against the organisation's objectives', with fairness metrics listed (#220); its generative-AI orientations call for a data processing agreement when model development is outsourced (#233) or a joint-controller agreement (#222), 'contractual assurances and documentation' on how the accuracy of development data was ensured (#230), reliable and regularly updated information on suppliers' datasets (#231, #232), probing of controls when a provider claims no personal data is processed (#223), and DPO review of data-sharing agreements with model providers (#226). The European Parliament's frameworks require that dependency on external experts or providers 'must be limited and monitored' (#179) and call for a charter for responsible data handling by IT providers (#184); a JRC report asks procurement to integrate 'technical specifications, contractual safeguards and evaluation criteria' and interoperability from the outset (#256, #257); and an AI Act recital asks the Commission to evaluate and promote best practice in public procurement of AI (#054). The ECA, which uses tools provided by the Commission, will define its functional and security requirements and work with the Commission to tailor those tools (#274, #276). Terms also run from supplier to public deployer: providers are expected to exclude prohibited uses in their terms of use (#133), and signatories of the transparency Code will forbid deployers to tamper with content markings (#238) while giving them access to logging policies and control over what is logged (#239).
themes.holders: EU institutions as contracting authorities and controllers, with their procurement and deployment staff and DPOs (EDPS documents); the European Parliament administration (holder not named); public administrations generally (JRC, holder not named); the Commission (recital); the ECA; providers and Code signatories (for supplier terms).
themes.binding: Mostly recommended ('should', 'will need to'); some EDPS passages restate statutory duties under Articles 28 and 29 of 'the Regulation' ([inference] the EU institutions' data protection regulation) (#222, #233); the European Parliament's 2024 framework uses 'must' but is internal and, per the coder note on #178, awaiting Bureau approval; the ECA's are commitments; the JRC's are recommendations; the AI Act passage is a recital; the Code's terms bind signatories who adhere. No consequence stated.
themes.checks: Metrics requested from the provider (#220): trigger, acquisition or deployment (the step is not specified in the quote); compared against, 'the organisation's objectives'; metric, a set supplied by the provider, with fairness metrics such as false-positive-rate parity, false-negative-rate parity and calibration listed in the note; who, the organisation requests and the provider supplies; what happens with the result, not stated. Accuracy of development data (#230): trigger, use of a third-party system or datasets; compared against, the supplier's documented procedures; metric, not stated; who, the EU institution obtains assurances; result, not stated. Procurement 'evaluation criteria' (#256) are named but not specified. Monitoring of dependency on suppliers (#179): metric and holder not stated. Logging (#239) gives deployers control over logs of output data but says nothing about reviewing them.

quotes.quote: the organisation should request from the provider a set of metrics that will allow for the evaluation of the AI system against the organisation’s objectives
contractual assurances and documentation must be obtained on the procedures used to ensure the accuracy of the data used for the development of the system.
This will require the integration of appropriate technical specifications, contractual safeguards and evaluation criteria into procurement procedures.
Dependency on external experts or external service providers must be limited and monitored.

themes.theme: Marking, labelling and detection across the content value chain
themes.definition: Arrangements under Article 50 of the AI Act for marking AI-generated content, making it detectable and keeping labels intact as content passes between model providers, system providers, deployers and distributors.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Article 50 guidelines say providers 'must rely on publicly-available industry standard detection solutions that allow any third party to implement detection' (#172), and a provider that depends on another actor for detection 'must ensure' that the solution complies and that detection results are displayed properly (#173). System providers may rely on marking done by an upstream model provider or a third party if it complies (#167), and the transparency Code likewise lets downstream providers rely on testing by upstream or third-party providers 'without prejudice to the ultimate responsibility' of the signatory (#243, per the note). Model providers are encouraged to mark at model level to help downstream compliance (#169, #177, #248), standardised visual indicators are recommended (#170), and perceptible marks are allowed to help deployers label deep fakes (#171); further down the chain, deployers should use contractual conditions with distributing partners so labels are displayed (#175), hosting services and platforms, though not liable under the AI Act, are 'strongly encouraged' to preserve marks (#176), and Code signatories are encouraged to collaborate with distributors (#250). Code signatories will implement an interoperable detection solution by 2 February 2027 (#249), publish how to integrate and access detection (#240), cooperate with the Commission on interoperability standards (#241), share information on transparency technologies with the AI Office and Board (#244), cooperate with competent authorities (#247), and forbid deployers to tamper with markings (#238). Public bodies appear only as possible deployers [inference, as the coder notes say].
themes.holders: Providers of generative AI systems and models; upstream model providers and third-party marking providers; deployers producing deep fakes or published text; hosting services, platforms and distributors; Code signatories; the Commission, AI Office and Board as recipients.
themes.binding: The guidelines interpret statutory Article 50 duties ('must'; per the coder field, fines under para 152); the Code's 'will' binds signatories, but adherence is voluntary; much is 'encouraged' or 'recommended'; platforms are expressly not responsible or liable under the AI Act for preserving marks.
themes.checks: Checks on marking and detection solutions (#167, #173, #243): trigger, not stated ([inference] before a provider relies on another's solution); compared against, Article 50(2) and (5) requirements; metric or threshold, not stated in these passages; who, the upstream or third-party provider tests and the downstream provider relies on that while staying responsible; what happens with the result, reliance is allowed 'so long as those solutions comply' (note on #243), and detection results must be displayed in line with Article 50(5) (#173).

quotes.quote: To ens ure full interoperability, providers must rely on publicly-available industry standard detection solution s that allow any third party to implement detection
They are, therefore, strongly encouraged to preserve the marking and labelling implemented pursuant to Article 50 AI Act

Signatories who are downstream providers of generative AI systems may rely on the results of testing performed by an upstream model provider or a third-party provider of marking and detection solutions
Signatories will implement an interoperability solution for their detection mechanisms by 2 February 202 7 by implementing one or more of the following

themes.definition: Recommendations that public administrations and Member States build, and reach out to, a market of start-ups and innovative suppliers for public-sector AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: The JRC handbook proposes promoting EU GovTech start-ups (#152), Member States joining forces to support GovTech companies (#157), public administrations keeping 'abreast of' and actively reaching out to innovative companies (#158), and specific procurement frameworks for start-ups, citing per the note the negotiated procedure without prior publication used during the pandemic (#159). The later JRC report repeats the call to adapt procurement 'to lower barriers for start-ups' (#253) and calls collaboration with 'trusted suppliers and partners' essential (#258), without saying how suppliers come to be trusted (note). The coders flagged several of these passages as doubtful in scope because they concern market development rather than governance of a tool. [inference] They pull against the procurement theme: these passages aim to loosen procurement for new suppliers, while the same JRC report asks procurement to carry contractual safeguards and evaluation criteria (#256) and the European Parliament asks for limited dependency on external providers (#179).
themes.holders: Public administrations; Member States; holder often not stated.
themes.binding: Recommendations, suggestions ('could be envisaged') and encouragement; nothing binding. No consequence stated.

quotes.quote: Public sector administrations are encouraged to keep abreast of and actively reach out to innovative companies whose available AI solutions could be beneficial to them.
Specific procurement frameworks and conditions dedicated to support start -ups could be envisaged

Providing support for a stronger EU AI ecosystem will entail adapting procurement and administrative processes to lower barriers for start-ups and better align public sector needs with innovative market solutions.
Collaboration with trusted suppliers and partners is essential to facilitate experimentation with and adoption of AI

themes.theme: Shared templates, typologies, standards and interoperability requirements
themes.definition: Common forms, code lists, criteria, specifications and interoperability requirements that put different actors on the same reference.
themes.what_is_set_out: In the AI Act, common specifications are a shared reference that Member States can challenge, with the Commission assessing and possibly amending them (#085), and the Board may develop 'common criteria and a shared understanding' among operators and authorities, including benchmarks (#116); the prohibited-practices guidelines present themselves as a shared reference for harmonised enforcement (#136). The Omnibus adds two shared forms: a simplified technical-documentation form for SMEs and small mid-caps that notified bodies 'shall accept' (#185), and the Annex XIV list of codes and types of AI systems that conformity assessment bodies must use (#210); the training-data Summary template links model versions and their Summaries along the value chain (#211). For public administrations, a JRC report states that AI solutions 'must be able to interact effectively with existing technologies and platforms', without citing a legal basis (#255), and that interoperability should be written into procurement specifications from the outset (#257), and the JRC handbook proposes national repositories of 'standards, guidelines and performance metrics' (#156). The ECA commits to align its data classification with its auditees, especially the Commission (#273), and its compliance practice with emerging EU-wide standards (#277).
themes.holders: The Commission; the Board; Member States; market surveillance authorities; notified and conformity assessment bodies; SMEs and small mid-caps; general-purpose model providers; public administrations (often not named); the ECA.
themes.binding: Statutory for common specifications, the simplified form and the Annex XIV codes; a mandatory template field (#211); the Board's role is permissive ('may'); recommendations (JRC); institutional commitments (ECA).
themes.checks: Benchmarks (#116) and 'performance metrics' (#156) are named, but neither passage says what they measure, who applies them, against what threshold, or with what result (the coder note on #156 says performance metrics are not defined and their use in evaluating tools is not stated).

quotes.location: p. 38, Art. 1(43) (AI Act Annex XIV point 4)
quotes.quote: Conformity assessment bodies shall use the lists of codes, categories and corresponding types of AI systems set out in this Annex when specifying the types of AI systems in the application for designation

facilitate the development of common criteria and a shared understanding among market operators and competent authorities of the relevant concepts provided for in this Regulation, including by contributing to the development of benchmarks
AI solutions must be able to interact effectively with existing technologies and platforms, to allow for seamless integration and functionality.
dedicated national repositories of standards, guidelines and performance metrics should be envisaged in combination with the above

themes.theme: EU database and public lists under the AI Act
themes.definition: The shared EU register of high-risk AI systems and the public lists of bodies and sandboxes that the AI Act requires.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Commission, with the Member States, must set up and maintain an EU database holding information on high-risk AI systems, which per the coder note covers systems registered under Articles 49 and 60 and those claimed not to be high-risk under Article 6(3)-(4) (#003). The Commission 'should be the controller' of the database, and per the note its set-up should include functional specifications and an independent audit report (#049). Three further public lists connect actors: notified bodies with their identification numbers and activities (#078), planned and existing sandboxes, published by the AI Office per the note 'to encourage more interaction' and cross-border cooperation (#100), and each Member State's fundamental-rights bodies (#012). The prohibited-practices guidelines add that law-enforcement remote biometric identification systems go into a 'secure non-public section' with limited information and access (#126). The duties to register, and what must be published from the database, are not set out in these passages.
themes.holders: The Commission (with Member States) as builder and controller; the AI Office (sandbox list); Member States (list of fundamental-rights bodies). Who registers is referred to but not set out here.
themes.binding: Statutory (Arts 35, 57, 71 and 77); recital 'should' for the controller role; the guidelines restate. No consequence stated.

quotes.quote: The Commission shall, in collaboration with the Member States, set up and maintain an EU database containing information referred to in paragraphs 2 and 3 of this Article concerning high-risk AI systems
The Commission should be the controller of the EU database, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2018/1725.
The AI Office shall make publicly available a list of planned and existing sandboxes and keep it up to date
RBI systems used for the purpose of law enforcement will be registered in a se cure non -public section of the database, with limited information and limited access to that information.
